note: Gilgamesh is a semi-legendary Early Dynastic king of Uruk; if historical, his reign is usually placed around c. 2800–2500 BCE without firm birth or death dates.
2334 BCE reflects the conventional Middle Chronology start of Sargon's reign rather than his birth year; exact birth and death dates are unattested.
2112 BCE is the conventional Middle Chronology accession year of Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, not his birth year.
Hammurabi's birth year is unrecorded and inferred from his Middle Chronology reign (c. 1792–1750 BCE); short and ultra-short chronologies differ by decades.
Imhotep served under Pharaoh Djoser in the Third Dynasty, whose reign dates vary across Egyptological chronologies (c. 27th century BCE); birth and death years are unknown.
Hatshepsut's birth year is estimated from the chronology of the Eighteenth Dynasty; her reign is dated approximately 1479–1458 BCE.
Akhenaten's birth year is approximate; his 17-year reign is generally placed c. 1353–1336 BCE with minor debate over a possible coregency.
Ancient traditions vary widely on Homer's date and identity; modern scholarship places the composition of the Homeric epics roughly in the late 8th or early 7th century BCE.
Scholars disagree sharply on Zoroaster's era, ranging from c. 1500–1000 BCE on linguistic grounds to the traditional c. 628–551 BCE.
563–483 BCE is the older scholarly convention; recent scholarship frequently places the Buddha's parinirvana closer to c. 480–400 BCE.
Traditional Jain dates (599–527 BCE) are debated alongside shorter chronologies linking Mahavira's lifetime with the revised dating of the Buddha (5th century BCE).
Laozi's historicity and dates are uncertain; traditional accounts make him an elder contemporary of Confucius in the 6th century BCE, while the Daodejing shows Warring States layers.
Birth and death years of Sun Wu are unattested in contemporary records and derived from later traditional chronologies of the late Spring and Autumn period.
Kautilya (Chanakya) is traditionally associated with Chandragupta Maurya (late 4th century BCE), but his exact lifespan is unknown and the Arthashastra shows multi-century redaction.
Chandragupta Maurya's reign began c. 321 BCE, but his birth year (c. 340 BCE) and exact death date are inferred from later classical and Jain sources.
257–179 BCE reflects traditional Vietnamese chronicle dates for the Au Lac polity rather than attested birth and death years of Thuc Phan.
Kalidasa's exact lifespan is undocumented; scholarly consensus places his floruit during the Gupta era, most commonly under Chandragupta II (c. 375–415 CE).
The Neolithic transition occurred independently across multiple regions over millennia starting roughly c. 10,000–9000 BCE in the Fertile Crescent.
Proto-cuneiform administrative tablets from Uruk IV date approximately to c. 3400–3200 BCE based on stratigraphy and radiocarbon calibration.
The sramana movements in the Gangetic plain emerged broadly between the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.
Early Sumerian Gilgamesh poems date to the Ur III period (c. 2100 BCE), while the Standard Babylonian Akkadian version by Sin-leqi-unninni dates to c. 1300–1000 BCE.
The Rigveda was transmitted orally for centuries; linguistic dating generally places its core hymns c. 1500–1200 BCE.
The core divination text of the Zhouyi dates to the early Western Zhou period (c. 1000–750 BCE), with the Ten Wings commentaries added in the Warring States and Han eras.
The Iliad's oral composition and textual fixation are broadly placed in the mid-to-late 8th century BCE.
The principal early Upanishads (Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya) were composed over several centuries roughly c. 700–500 BCE.
The Old Avestan Gathas may date to c. 1200–1000 BCE, while the surviving Sasanian written redaction is much later.
Traditionally dated to c. 500 BCE, though many historians place the received text's compilation in the Warring States period (4th–3rd century BCE).
Early manuscript witnesses (Guodian bamboo slips) date to c. 300 BCE, indicating formation across the 4th century BCE or earlier.
Traditionally attributed to Kautilya (c. 300 BCE), the extant Sanskrit text shows editorial layers extending into the early centuries CE.
The Pali Dhammapada verses were transmitted orally before being committed to writing in Sri Lanka in the 1st century BCE.
Embedded in the Mahabharata, the Bhagavad Gita is generally dated by scholars between the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE.

Traditional Vietnamese sources place Trieu Thi Trinh's birth in 226 CE based on her reported age of 22 at the 248 CE uprising; contemporary Chinese records (Sanguozhi/Jinshu) do not record her birth year.
503 CE is the conventional traditional birth year of Ly Bi in Vietnamese historiography; contemporary Liang chronicles focus on his 542–548 CE uprising without recording his exact birth date.
525 CE is an approximate traditional estimate; only his military leadership (545–550 CE) and death (571 CE) are firmly attested in historical chronicles.
670 CE is a conventional estimate for Mai Thuc Loan's birth; Tang and Vietnamese sources primarily attest his 722 CE Hoan Chau rebellion.
850 CE is an approximate estimate; his 905 CE assumption of power at Dai La and 907 CE death are firmly recorded, while his exact birth year is unattested.
Khuc Hao's birth year is unrecorded in surviving chronicles; his tenure as Jiedushi of Jinghai Circuit (907–917 CE) and death in 917 CE are attested.
Some older compilations cite 1720 as Le Huu Trac's birth year, while modern Vietnamese scholarship and UNESCO (300th anniversary commemoration in 2024) adopt 1724.
Hoang Hoa Tham's birth year is variously cited as 1858 or c. 1846 across modern Vietnamese archival and biographical sources.
